rationale:
The example `requirements.sdk.graph.hierarchical-paths` describes a concrete case. A requirement named `a.b.c` is represented as `ReviewNodeId::Requirement(vec!["a","b","c"])`, and its `node_path` is `["requirement","a","b","c"]`.

The test `crates/trust-but-verify/src/graph/validation_tests.rs#fn[enum_node_ids_distinguish_requirements_and_source_items_in_one_domain]` carries a `{test}` reference to this example. It defines a local `ReviewNodeId` enum with `Requirement(Vec<String>)` and `Source{file,selector}` variants, which matches the "enum above". It also defines a `ReviewDomain` whose `node_path` prefixes requirement parts with `"requirement"`.

The test builds exactly the example's identity, `ReviewNodeId::Requirement(vec!["a","b","c"])`, and calls `Domain::node_path`. It asserts `path.segments() == ["requirement","a","b","c"]`, which is the example's expected outcome.

It also checks the cited `node_path_method` obligations:
- Calling `node_path` twice on the same domain gives equal paths.
- A fresh `ReviewDomain::default()` gives an equal path, so the mapping is stable across instances.
- Requirement and source identities give distinct paths: `["requirement","sdk","errors"]` and `["source","src/lib.rs","fn[validate]"]`.

Because the example describes what a user-defined `Domain` implementation does, a test-local implementation is the appropriate way to verify it. I found no unasserted outcome and no assertion that contradicts the example.
